epics.title: mini-boss — a self-contained mind with a browser terminal and a Telegram surface
epics.description:
One repo, one compose file, four containers. A mind that runs a harness CLI, serves a tmux-backed browser terminal, answers Telegram, and speaks — with no hive-comms, no hive-lucent, no broker, no gateway, no external nervous system.

This supersedes the earlier 'Telegram surface over an existing Claude Code agent' sketch. The scope grew for one reason: the tmux-backed terminal turned out to be the better primary surface, and everything needed to run it is already built and proven in hive-edge-minds and the terminal repo. This project is mostly subtraction — lifting that machinery out of the hive and cutting its dependency on the gateway. Target hosts: Daniel's work laptop, and any machine that should have a mind without joining the hive. Note the project has since been retargeted to native Linux for a lab box, VPN-only, on a machine that is not his, with a setup that installs nothing.

Four containers on one docker network, one compose up. Only Caddy publishes a port; everything else is internal.

Decisions taken: the name is mini-boss; both codex and claude adapters ship from day one; there is no session rotation, relying on the harness's own compaction; the terminal is consumed as a published image from the terminal repo; the database is two SQLite files in volumes with no database container; the front door is Caddy, single origin, plain HTTP on localhost:8430; and the phone is served by Telegram rather than the browser terminal.
epics.requirements:
Why four containers. mind and web are separate because of lifecycle: the mind container holds live tmux sessions and running harness processes, so restarting it destroys conversations mid-turn, while the web container is stateless and gets redeployed constantly for a CSS tweak, a keybinding or a mobile viewport fix — merged, every front-end iteration kills every live pane, and that single fact settles it. Supporting: the images share nothing, since one is Ubuntu with Node and the harness CLI and the other a Python slim with static assets, so a UI change would rebuild the harness layer; and the mind needs the host root bind-mounted to be an operator mind while the web container must not have it. voice is separate because of model weights and optional CUDA, so the mind image stays buildable on a laptop with no GPU and a host that does not want voice simply does not start the service. caddy is separate because it is a stock upstream image with no code of ours in it. The cost of the split is one extra network hop on the terminal WebSocket, which is a loopback hop on a shared docker network and is not measurable against a human typing.

The eleven-route contract. The terminal container talks to hive-comms through exactly one environment variable and calls a small closed set of routes, so the mind container implements that same set, the variable is repointed at it, and the web container works unmodified — no fork, no divergence, and the terminal repo stays shared between the hive build and this one. The routes: the mind picker returning this one mind; the session list for the tile switcher; session create; the SSE event stream carrying assistant text for the speaker; send a chat turn; suspend; resume; end the session and kill the harness; the terminal pty bridge with columns and rows; the terminal-voice route carrying transcript prose for the speaker; and a timestamp write from the Stop hook. The mind picker looks vestigial in a single-mind build and is kept anyway, because it is what lets the same web container point at either a hive gateway or a mini-boss without a code path per deployment. The turn-record route is narrowed here: in the hive it fed the rotation ledger and kept last_active current for pty turns, and since rotation is gone only the second remains — but it still has to exist, because without it every terminal session reads as stale forever in the tile switcher's relative-age column. Voice is a second base URL with a TTS and an STT route.
epics.acceptance_criteria: Build order: the mind container answers the contract, verified with curl and a websocket client and no browser yet; the terminal works, with the seed fix landed and tagged, the GHCR workflow publishing, the image pulled, the gateway variable repointed, and a tile attaching to a real pane with resize and reattach behaving; Caddy on a single origin with web at the root, voice at its two routes, and mind reachable only from web; Telegram, with the bot in-process, the allowlist enforced, and a turn typed in Telegram landing in the same session the tile shows; voice, with Piper and faster-whisper and the speaker and mic live in the tile; and a one-command install, with the example environment filled, a compose up, the first user seeded, and the README written.
epics.qa_tests: Every item in the carried-over list was a bug once, so each is a regression to protect rather than a precaution. The pty bridge's exact-match tmux targets in particular: prefix matching will otherwise let one session id answer for another's pane.

features.title: Container 1 — mind
features.description:
Ubuntu 24.04 with Python, Node, both harness CLIs, tmux, git and gh, lifted from the edge repo's Dockerfile minus Playwright and the hive's vendored dependencies. One Python process gathering the FastAPI app and the Telegram bot — one log stream, one thing to restart.

What it owns: the session table in SQLite on a named volume, where sessions are rows carrying id, label, harness conversation id, last_active and owner — the piece hive-comms used to own, collapsed in here. tmux, where a conversation lives in a session on a dedicated socket and a browser tile is a client attached with a detaching attach, so closing the tab detaches the view without touching the conversation and re-attaching joins the same session rather than starting a rival CLI, with tmux owning the screen model and history so there is no VT emulator, no scrollback ring and no snapshot painter on this side. The pty bridge, moving raw bytes between xterm.js and the pty, with setsid and TIOCSCTTY so a resize's SIGWINCH actually reaches the app, a NUL-byte heartbeat every five seconds so half-open mobile sockets are detectable, and exact-match tmux targets. Both harness adapters, selected by config, which differ in more than a flag: Claude takes a model on its command line and picks resume against session-id by whether a transcript file exists, while Codex takes no model argument at all — its pane reads the model from a generated config file — mints its own thread id, and files a rollout named for it. The Telegram bot in-process, with a sender allowlist on a hard-coded numeric user id checked before anything else. Prompt composition, which in the hive lives in the gateway and here must be added rather than deleted, composing a system prompt from a local soul file plus whatever the hooks inject — the one place the minimal build adds code. And explaining a harness that dies: tmux returns success because it started the process fine, and a harness failing on a bad key prints its complaint into a pane that is then destroyed, so the pane is kept briefly with remain-on-exit set from a config file so it is in force before the session exists, and its scrollback captured, so the browser is told the reason rather than getting an empty tile that flickers and stops.
features.requirements:
Mounts: host root at /host as the operator-mind pattern, a named volume for the session database, and a named volume for the harness config directories — the container's own rather than the operator's. Credentials come from the inference proxy named in the environment file, so nothing is shared with or copied from a logged-in command line: sharing the operator's harness config would race their own CLI on OAuth refresh, and mounting it over the image would mask the hooks shipped inside.

Carried over from the terminal work, because each one was a bug once: the agent-view disable flag in the pane for the claude harness, because the agent view is a second session picker inside a surface that already has one and it re-hosts the conversation in a nested pty at the wrong geometry; Codex minting its own thread ids and being unable to adopt an externally chosen one, so the provider-native id is persisted and a failed or incomplete turn clears it so the next turn never resumes a broken one; a fresh codex terminal launching bare codex rather than a pre-minted thread, because the app-server's thread-start returns an id and an intended rollout path without writing the rollout so a resume against it fails with no saved session found — poll the sessions directory for the rollout codex itself writes on the first real turn and take the id from its filename; checking the rollout still exists under this config home before reattaching to a stored thread id, since a redeploy onto a fresh volume otherwise hands back a pane that dies within a second of tmux starting it; reading the profile from the config file rather than passing a profile flag, because app-server rejects it outright unlike plain codex; POSIX spawns using start_new_session and killpg, because the node wrapper's rust child must not orphan to PID 1; and the harness process ending only on the session delete, because a terminal is never reaped for being unattached — that is the normal state between tiles and a turn in flight must survive a closed tab — with a reaper running only to drop registry entries whose harness has already exited.
features.acceptance_criteria: Step one of the build order: the mind answers the eleven-route contract, verified with curl and a websocket client before any browser is involved.
features.qa_tests: The exact-match tmux target is the one to test deliberately, because prefix matching lets one session id answer for another's pane. The remain-on-exit capture is the other: a harness that dies on a bad key must produce a readable reason rather than an empty flickering tile.

stories.title: Implement the eleven routes and the session table
stories.description: FastAPI plus a SQLite session table on a named volume, carrying id, label, harness conversation id, last_active and owner. The piece hive-comms used to own, collapsed in.
stories.requirements: All eleven, including the vestigial mind picker so one web container serves either deployment.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Verified with curl and a websocket client, no browser.
stories.qa_tests: Each route answers. The mind picker returns this one mind. The turn-record route keeps last_active current, without which every session reads as stale forever in the tile switcher.

stories.title: Build the tmux-backed pty bridge
stories.description: Raw bytes between xterm.js and the pty. The conversation lives in tmux; a tile is a client attached with a detaching attach.
stories.requirements: setsid plus TIOCSCTTY so a resize's SIGWINCH reaches the app; a NUL heartbeat every five seconds; exact-match tmux targets on every lookup; start_new_session and killpg on spawn and kill.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Closing the tab detaches without touching the conversation, and reattaching joins the same session.
stories.qa_tests: A resize repaints — without a controlling terminal, a resize sets winsize and signals nobody. A prefix-matched target can answer for another session's pane, so the exact form is asserted. A turn in flight survives a closed tab.

stories.title: Ship both harness adapters, selected by config
stories.description: They differ in more than a flag. Claude takes a model on its command line and picks resume against session-id by whether a transcript exists. Codex takes no model argument — its pane reads the model from a generated config file — mints its own thread id, and files a rollout named for it.
stories.requirements: Both from day one.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Either harness runs a pane from the same code path.
stories.qa_tests: A claude pane resumes by transcript existence. A codex pane's thread id is discovered from the rollout filename rather than pre-minted, because app-server's thread-start writes no rollout and a resume against its id fails with no saved session found.

stories.title: Guard a stored codex thread id against a missing rollout
stories.description: Before reattaching, check the rollout still exists under this config home. A redeploy onto a fresh volume otherwise hands back a pane that dies within a second of tmux starting it.
stories.requirements: Checked, with a fallback to the fresh-terminal path.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A redeploy does not produce a pane that dies immediately.
stories.qa_tests: With the rollout removed, the stored id is discarded and a fresh terminal starts instead.

stories.title: Compose the system prompt locally
stories.description: The one place the minimal build adds code rather than deleting it. In the hive this lives in the gateway; here there is no gateway, so the mind composes from a local soul file plus whatever the hooks inject.
stories.requirements: A local soul file; hook-injected context.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A turn carries the mind's identity with no gateway involved.
stories.qa_tests: A cold session answers as the mind the soul file describes. Hook-injected context reaches the model, which means additionalContext rather than systemMessage.

stories.title: Capture a dying harness's complaint instead of flickering an empty tile
stories.description: tmux returns success because it started the process fine, and a harness failing on a bad key prints its complaint into a pane that is then destroyed. Keep the pane briefly with remain-on-exit, set from a config file so it is in force before the session exists, and capture its scrollback.
stories.requirements: remain-on-exit from a config file, not set after the fact.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The browser is told the reason.
stories.qa_tests: A harness given a bad key produces a readable reason in the browser rather than an empty tile that flickers and stops. Setting remain-on-exit after the session exists is too late, which is why it comes from the config file.

stories.title: Run the Telegram bot in-process with a numeric allowlist
stories.description: Gathered alongside the FastAPI app so there is one log stream and one thing to restart. The sender allowlist is on a hard-coded numeric user id, checked before anything else, with a silent drop.
stories.requirements: Numeric id, checked first.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A turn typed in Telegram lands in the same session the tile shows.
stories.qa_tests: An unlisted sender is dropped silently. A listed one's turn appears in the tile's session. The id is validated as a number at setup, because a handle there produces a bot that silently ignores its owner — which looks exactly like a bot nobody has messaged.

features.title: No session rotation
features.description: Deliberate, and the largest reason mini-boss is a small project. In the hive, rotation exists because a conversation hits the context ceiling, and carry-forward composes a successor's opening turn out of lucent's memory. mini-boss has no lucent, so that machinery cannot come across intact — and the degraded version, asking the harness to summarize itself, buys little that the harness's own in-session compaction does not already do.
features.requirements: No rotation, no carry-forward, no staged-rotation markers, no arm-and-fire hook pair, no late-turns ledger, no rotated-to close code. A session ends when Daniel ends it.
features.acceptance_criteria: This deletes the single most intricate subsystem in hive-edge-minds.
features.qa_tests: Per the standard, a removal earns no test that it is gone. What is testable is that the harness's own compaction carries a long conversation, which is judged by using it.

stories.title: Rely on the harness's own in-session compaction
stories.description: No rotation subsystem at all. A session ends when Daniel ends it.
stories.requirements: Nothing to build — the absence is the decision.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A long conversation stays usable without a rotation.
stories.qa_tests: Judged by running a long conversation. No test asserts the absence of the rotation machinery, per the standard.

features.title: Container 2 — web, consumed as a published image
features.description:
The terminal is already its own private repository, and already decoupled from the hive: its dependencies are a short list, it imports no hive code, and its entire coupling to the nervous system is one environment variable and the eleven routes. That is a contract, not a dependency. So mini-boss's compose pulls the published image at a pinned semver tag, never latest — the hive and the laptop can sit on different versions, and neither moves because master got a push on a Saturday. The terminal repo's own compose keeps a source build with a bind mount, so development stays live-reload source and only consumers get the artifact.

Rejected alternatives: a submodule pins a commit that nothing reminds you is stale, so one source of truth silently behaves like two, and it breaks a plain clone. A vendored copy drifts within a month and makes every terminal fix a two-repo change.

What terminal already gives us: login against its own SQLite user table with a signed session cookie; the xterm.js tile with vendored xterm.js, the fit addon and the webgl addon, vendored rather than from a CDN; server-side tile labels so they follow the user across devices; the session switcher; mobile viewport handling; the speaker, which strips fenced code blocks from what it sends to TTS while leaving them on screen and silences an unterminated fence rather than speaking half a command; and a WebSocket proxy that forwards TEXT as TEXT and BINARY as BINARY, since the resize control channel rides as TEXT frames and must not be transcoded.
features.requirements:
Needed: a GitHub Actions workflow in the terminal repo that builds and pushes to GHCR on tag, and a one-time registry login with a PAT on each mini-boss host. The repo stays private — trading that for dodging a one-time login is a bad trade.

The one change terminal needs: its lifespan calls the auth-db initialiser but deliberately not the first-user seeder, with a comment explaining that the hive site owns the shared auth db so users already exist by startup. In mini-boss there is no hive site, so the container comes up with an empty users table and no way to log in. The fix is to call the seeder in lifespan too — it is already idempotent and returns immediately when the seed credentials are unset, so the hive deployment is unaffected. One line, and it only surfaced because a second consumer exists. mini-boss then points the database path at its own volume, leaves the cookie domain unset for a host-only cookie, and supplies the two seed variables for first launch.
features.acceptance_criteria: No fork and no divergence: the web container works unmodified against either a hive gateway or a mini-boss.
features.qa_tests: The seeder fix is testable both ways: with the seed credentials set it creates a user, and with them unset it returns immediately so the hive deployment is unchanged. The WebSocket proxy's frame-type preservation matters because the resize channel rides as TEXT and transcoding it breaks resize silently.

stories.title: Call seed_first_user in terminal's lifespan
stories.description: One line. Already idempotent and returns immediately when the seed credentials are unset, so the hive deployment is unaffected. It only surfaced because a second consumer exists.
stories.requirements: Idempotent, and a no-op when unset.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A fresh mini-boss can be logged into.
stories.qa_tests: With the seed credentials set, a user is created and a second start creates nothing further. With them unset, nothing is created and the hive deployment is unchanged.

stories.title: Add the GHCR publish workflow and pin the image by tag
stories.description: Builds and pushes on tag. mini-boss pulls a pinned semver tag, never latest, so the hive and the laptop can sit on different versions. The repo stays private, so each host does a one-time registry login with a PAT.
stories.requirements: Pinned tag, private repo, one-time login per host.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Neither deployment moves because master got a Saturday push.
stories.qa_tests: A tag produces an image. A compose pull at the pinned tag gets that image and no other. A submodule or a vendored copy would both fail this — one pins a commit nothing reminds you is stale, the other drifts within a month.

stories.title: Repoint the gateway variable at the mind and verify a tile attaches
stories.description: Step two of the build order. A tile attaches to a real pane, and resize and reattach behave.
stories.requirements: The web container unmodified.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The eleven-route contract holds against the mind.
stories.qa_tests: A tile attaches, resize repaints, a reattach joins the same pane. The proxy forwards TEXT as TEXT and BINARY as BINARY, since the resize control channel rides as TEXT and must not be transcoded.

features.title: Terminal voice
features.description: A conversation hosted in a pty publishes no assistant events, because the bridge moves rendered bytes rather than structured text. So the mind tails the harness's own transcript file and posts each new prose block to the terminal-voice route.
features.requirements: A tailer opens at end-of-file when it first sees a conversation, so attaching to a session with hours of history does not read the past aloud. Only text blocks are read: thinking is written empty to disk regardless, and reading a diff aloud is not speech.
features.acceptance_criteria: The tile's speaker works on a pty-hosted conversation.
features.qa_tests: Attaching to a session with history reads nothing of the past. A new prose block is spoken. A thinking block and a tool result are not. The browser strips fenced code blocks from what it sends to the voice server while leaving them on screen, and silences an unterminated fence rather than speaking half a command.

stories.title: Tail the harness transcript and post prose blocks
stories.description: Opening at end-of-file on first sight, and reading only text blocks.
stories.requirements: No history read aloud; thinking and tool output skipped.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The speaker works without the bridge publishing events.
stories.qa_tests: A session with hours of history reads nothing on attach. A fresh prose block is posted. Thinking blocks are written empty to disk regardless, so skipping them is correct rather than a limitation.

features.title: Container 3 — voice, optional
features.description: Not Chatterbox. Something lighter that runs on CPU and uses a GPU when there is one. TTS is Piper: ONNX, faster than real time on a laptop CPU, one voice model is tens of megabytes, no CUDA required, with quality below Chatterbox and above every other CPU option. STT is faster-whisper, base or small int8 on CPU and medium on GPU, with the same API either way so the device is a config value rather than a code path.
features.requirements: It exposes a TTS and an STT route with the same request and response shapes the current voice server uses, so the web client is unchanged. GPU is a compose override rather than a second image. If the service is not running the tile degrades to a terminal with no speaker — the mic and speaker controls go dark and nothing errors.
features.acceptance_criteria: The mind image stays buildable on a laptop with no GPU, and a host that does not want voice simply does not start the service.
features.qa_tests: With voice stopped, the tile still works and the controls go dark rather than erroring. The request and response shapes match the existing voice server, which is what keeps the web client unmodified.

stories.title: Build the Piper and faster-whisper voice container
stories.description: Same route shapes as the current voice server, so the web client is unchanged. GPU as a compose override rather than a second image.
stories.requirements: CPU-capable by default, GPU optional.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The speaker and mic are live in the tile.
stories.qa_tests: TTS and STT answer on CPU. The GPU override uses the card. With the service stopped, the tile degrades silently rather than erroring.

features.title: Container 4 — caddy, and why plain HTTP is correct
features.description:
Caddy is the single front door, serving the web container at the root and proxying the two voice routes, so the browser makes only same-origin calls — no mixed-content rule fires and no CORS configuration exists. It is also the only container that publishes a port; mind, web and voice stay internal.

It serves plain HTTP on localhost:8430, and that is correct rather than a compromise. The microphone is the constraint that would otherwise force TLS, because getUserMedia only runs in a secure context and a LAN IP from a phone is not one, so the mic button dies silently there. But localhost IS a secure context by specification. The browser that uses mini-boss is the laptop's own, so the mic, the clipboard and service workers all work with no certificate, no local CA and no trust-store install. The phone is served by the Telegram bot rather than the browser terminal — that is the division of surfaces: at the console, the tile; away from it, Telegram. Nothing about the browser terminal breaks over plain localhost HTTP, since the WebSocket is on the same origin and the speaker and mic are live.
features.requirements: Only Caddy publishes 8430. Internal and unpublished: mind on 8431, web on 8432, voice on 8433 — chosen to miss everything already running on Daniel's boxes.
features.acceptance_criteria: No certificate, no local CA, no trust-store install, and the mic works.
features.qa_tests: The mic button works on localhost. It would not on a LAN IP, which is why the phone is Telegram's job. Only one port is published, verified from outside the docker network.

stories.title: Configure Caddy as the single origin on localhost:8430
stories.description: Web at the root, voice proxied, mind reachable only from web. The only container publishing a port.
stories.requirements: Same-origin only, so no mixed content and no CORS.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The mic, clipboard and service worker all work with no certificate.
stories.qa_tests: The mic works on localhost. mind, web and voice are unreachable from outside the docker network. The three internal ports avoid everything already running.

features.title: Data — two SQLite files, no database container
features.description: Daniel raised needing a database for auth. Agreed on the database; disagreed on the container. Both stores are SQLite files, each owned by exactly one container: the auth database owned by web, holding users, signed-cookie identities and terminal tile labels; and the sessions database owned by mind, holding session rows, harness conversation ids and last_active. Each lives in a named volume. Labels already share the auth database in the terminal repo, so this is not a new arrangement, just a differently-pointed database path.
features.requirements: A Postgres or MySQL container would add a service to supervise, a startup ordering dependency, a backup story and roughly 300 MB of image for a single-user, single-host mind whose largest table will hold dozens of rows. SQLite is what the hive already uses for sessions and is the right answer at this scale. The two files stay separate rather than merging into one shared volume: they have different owners and different lifecycles, and the whole point of the container split is that redeploying the web container cannot disturb mind state.
features.acceptance_criteria: Redeploying web leaves mind state untouched.
features.qa_tests: A web redeploy leaves live tmux sessions and the session table intact. Merging the volumes would break that, which is the reason they stay apart.

stories.title: Give each container its own SQLite volume
stories.description: auth.db owned by web, sessions.db owned by mind. Separate volumes, separate lifecycles.
stories.requirements: No database container.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A web redeploy cannot disturb mind state.
stories.qa_tests: Redeploy web mid-conversation: the pane survives and the session row is unchanged.

features.title: Windows, which means WSL2
features.description:
Docker Desktop runs its containers inside WSL2 regardless, so WSL2 is not a choice — it is where this runs either way. What is chosen is where the checkout lives and which daemon answers.

The setup script provisions rather than reports: it installs WSL2 if absent, installs Ubuntu if absent, installs the Docker engine inside the distribution, writes the environment file from five answers, and starts the stack. The rules live in a preflight module, with evidence collection split from a pure verdict, and a provision module mapping issue keys to repairs tagged with which side performs them; the PowerShell is thin because only two things genuinely need Windows — reading a secret without echoing it, and shelling into the distro.
features.requirements:
Three constraints shape it. Installing WSL2 needs elevation and a restart, so the script stops after that step and resumes on the next run rather than executing the rest against a machine that has not rebooted — and without administrator rights it changes nothing and says so, because a half-installed WSL leaves a machine that is neither what it was nor what it should be. A checkout on the Windows drive is relocated rather than refused, because bind mounts across the Windows mount are an order of magnitude slower and inotify never fires, and the copy leaves the Windows-side clone untouched so a failure costs nothing. And Docker Desktop is refused, which is load-bearing: its daemon runs in its own utility VM, so the operator mount at /host would give the mind that VM's filesystem instead of the distribution holding the operator's work — the same compose file, two entirely different minds.

The five answers are the login username and password, the proxy API key, the Telegram bot token, and the numeric Telegram user id. The cookie secret is generated rather than asked for. The Telegram id is validated as a number at setup, because the allowlist compares numbers and a handle there produces a bot that silently ignores its owner — which looks exactly like a bot nobody has messaged.
features.acceptance_criteria: A one-command install from five answers, resumable across the reboot WSL2 requires.
features.qa_tests: The Docker Desktop refusal is the one with a silent wrong outcome behind it: accepting it would mount the utility VM's filesystem as /host and produce a mind that looks right and operates the wrong machine. The id validation catches a bot that ignores its owner, which is indistinguishable from a bot nobody messaged.

stories.title: Write the preflight and provision modules with a pure verdict
stories.description: Evidence collection split from a pure verdict, and issue keys mapped to repairs tagged with which side performs them. The PowerShell is thin because only reading a secret without echoing it and shelling into the distro genuinely need Windows.
stories.requirements: A pure verdict, so the decision is testable without touching a machine.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The verdict function is testable in isolation.
stories.qa_tests: Given a set of collected evidence, the verdict is deterministic. The repair mapping names which side performs each.

stories.title: Stop after the WSL2 install and resume on the next run
stories.description: Installing WSL2 needs elevation and a restart. Without administrator rights the script changes nothing and says so, because a half-installed WSL leaves a machine that is neither what it was nor what it should be.
stories.requirements: Stop, resume, and refuse to change anything without elevation.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No machine is left half-installed.
stories.qa_tests: Without elevation, nothing is changed and the refusal says why. After the reboot, the next run continues rather than starting over.

stories.title: Relocate a checkout off the Windows drive
stories.description: Bind mounts across the Windows mount are an order of magnitude slower and inotify never fires. The copy leaves the Windows-side clone untouched, so a failure costs nothing.
stories.requirements: Relocated rather than refused.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The Windows-side clone is untouched.
stories.qa_tests: After a relocation, the original clone is intact and the running checkout is inside the distribution. A failure mid-copy leaves the original usable.

stories.title: Refuse Docker Desktop
stories.description: Load-bearing. Its daemon runs in its own utility VM, so the operator mount at /host would give the mind that VM's filesystem instead of the distribution holding the operator's work — the same compose file, two entirely different minds.
stories.requirements: Refused, with the reason stated.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The mind operates the machine the operator works on.
stories.qa_tests: With Docker Desktop's daemon answering, setup refuses and names the reason. Accepting it would produce a mind that looks right and operates the wrong filesystem, which is the silent failure.

stories.title: Validate the Telegram id as a number at setup
stories.description: The allowlist compares numbers, and a handle there produces a bot that silently ignores its owner — which looks exactly like a bot nobody has messaged.
stories.requirements: Validated at setup, not discovered at first message.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A handle is refused with an explanation.
stories.qa_tests: A non-numeric id is refused at setup. A numeric one is accepted and the bot answers its owner.

features.title: Security notes, deferred
features.description: Not part of the implementation. Recorded so it is not re-derived later. The mind is already on the machine with full dev capability, so the only new exposure is the communication layer: remote reachability is the change, since the terminal agent needs Daniel at the keyboard while the Telegram and browser agent can be driven from anywhere.
features.requirements:
The list: a sender allowlist on the numeric Telegram user id, checked first, with a silent drop — in the implementation above because it is three lines rather than because it is a security programme. The bot token in the OS credential store rather than the repo, which on Windows is Credential Manager or an ACL'd DPAPI blob, since a mode-600 file is the Linux equivalent and does not exist there. Pinning the bot identity by calling getMe at startup and refusing to run unless the bot id matches, so a swapped token is a different bot and fails immediately. An audit log of every inbound command — sender, timestamp, message — as the substrate for anomaly alerting on repeated dropped-sender hits, bursts of destructive git or filesystem operations, off-hours activity, update conflicts implying a second instance, and volume spikes, where any one is benign and a cluster is the alert. A kill switch, for which stopping the container is one. And 2FA on the Telegram account.

Prompt injection is the residual threat once identity is pinned, and it is not solvable at the model layer — the major labs have each said so publicly. Content-screening by an LLM is itself injectable, regex denylists have no reliable surface to match, and detection classifiers score in the low 90s clean and 60 to 70 under obfuscation. The architectural answer is to break one leg of the trifecta — untrusted content, sensitive data, external egress — per operation, and for a coding agent behind a remote channel the leg to cut is egress: a deterministic, non-model gate that refuses to let anything derived from tainted content reach a network send or a secret-touching shell command. Provenance stamping at fetch time, a no-tools sub-agent for summarizing untrusted content, and classifiers and canary tokens as tripwires feeding the log rather than as the wall.
features.acceptance_criteria:
Deliberately not doing, whenever this is picked up: confirmation gates on destructive actions, which are theatre against a hijacked channel since the attacker confirms their own actions and per-action nagging makes skipped permissions unusable; a working-directory cage, since the mind works across all repos by design; and output redaction, which the mind already handles.

Open: whether employer policy permits a remotely-reachable agent on the work machine at all. That one gates the install rather than the design — and the project has since been retargeted to a lab box that is not his, VPN-only, with a setup that installs nothing.
features.qa_tests: The bot-identity pin is the cheapest real control and is testable: a swapped token fails at startup rather than running as someone else's bot. The egress gate is the architectural answer and is deterministic by design, so it is testable without a model: content derived from a tainted fetch cannot reach a network send.
